strengths: Originality/significance: The paper offers an interesting connection between in-context learning, continual learning, and Bayesian metaplasticity. Tracking a second, per-state importance variable is a plausible and potentially useful way to improve fixed-capacity recurrent attention memories.

Soundness: The core Palimpsa recurrence is mathematically motivated, computationally local, and compatible with associative-scan implementations. The MQAR experiment provides a useful controlled ablation across two architectural families, eight seeds, and increasing sequence lengths; its results support the claim that metaplasticity can reduce interference.

Evaluation: Experiments span synthetic recall and 170M/760M language models. Fine-tuning from non-metaplastic checkpoints while preserving token budgets is practically relevant, and the 760M variants improve their corresponding baselines by about 0.6 average accuracy points.
Presentation: The paper is generally clear and well organized, with helpful diagrams, architecture descriptions, derivations, hyperparameter tables, and an appendix discussing implementation details.

Limitations/ethics: The authors candidly report substantial training and inference overhead, register/HBM bottlenecks, and the absence of a MesaNet comparison. The work raises no evident material ethical concern, although the impact discussion is mostly benefit-oriented.
weaknesses: Soundness: Several derivations do not fully support the claimed unified Bayesian framework. Most notably, Eq. 32 gives a Gated DeltaNet update with alpha multiplying only the retained state, whereas Table 1 places alpha around the entire delta-corrected state; the statement that these are equivalent by reparameterization is not demonstrated. The appendix also inconsistently omits the prior precision from the mean gradient in Eq. 15 while restoring it in Eqs. 20 and 23.

Soundness/originality: Palimpsa is not the exact variational solution suggested in parts of the main text. The method first derives a coupled Gaussian solution and then discards off-diagonal precision terms, an approximation stronger than merely selecting a diagonal variational covariance. Likewise, Mamba2 is only an approximate limiting case when importance stays near the prior, together with a beta-to-zero/value-rescaling construction; calling it simply a special case overstates the result.

Evidence: The language-model gains are small and reported without repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. At 170M, fully trained Palimpsa-D is worse than its non-metaplastic counterpart, and results are otherwise mixed. At 760M only fine-tuned metaplastic models are evaluated, so the evidence does not establish that metaplasticity consistently helps training from scratch.

Evidence/significance: The paper attributes improved LAMBADA perplexity to long-range memory, but provides no controlled context-length ablation or modern long-context language benchmark. Improvements on aggregate commonsense tasks do not isolate memory capacity, while MQAR alone is too synthetic to validate the broader claims about in-context catastrophic forgetting and remembering.

Efficiency: The abstract claims speeds comparable to Mamba1, but no Mamba1/Mamba2 throughput comparison is presented. The appendix instead reports approximately 3x training overhead at 760M and a 4x attention-kernel inference slowdown versus Simple GLA. End-to-end latency, memory consumption, and matched-hardware comparisons are missing.

Experimental comparability is insufficiently documented. Exact parameter counts are absent, architecture depth and value expansion differ substantially across models, and learning-rate selection favors the best rate per model across seeds and sequence sizes. More transparent compute/FLOP matching and tuning budgets are needed.

Reproducibility: Although some hyperparameters are provided, there is no Palimpsa code or kernel release reference and important details are missing, including exact model configurations and parameter counts, tokenizer and data version, optimizer settings, batch/sequence setup, evaluation harness and prompting, checkpoint-selection rules, and language-model seeds. The expensive 30B-token results would therefore be difficult to reproduce reliably.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper offers an interesting synthesis of Bayesian continual learning and gated linear attention. The dual-state Palimpsa update, interpretation of the precision state as per-parameter plasticity, and connections to Longhorn, DeltaNet, MesaNet, and Mamba2 are potentially useful conceptual contributions.

Soundness: The derivation begins from a coherent weighted-posterior objective and clearly identifies the diagonal-precision approximation needed for tractability. The resulting recurrence is explicit, and the appendix provides substantial algebraic detail.

The MQAR experiment is reasonably targeted to interference in fixed-size memories. It includes metaplasticity ablations, four learning rates, and eight seeds; Palimpsa-D shows a meaningful advantage at the longest tested sequence length.
The work goes beyond toy scale by training 170M- and 760M-parameter models and describes a fused associative-scan implementation. Training and inference overheads are reported rather than concealed.
Presentation is generally clear and well organized, with readable figures, a useful architecture-comparison table, and several architectural and optimization details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Soundness: The evidence does not establish the central claim that Palimpsa prevents both catastrophic forgetting and catastrophic remembering. MQAR tests retention of associations, but there is no experiment with stale, changed, or conflicting associations that measures the ability to forget and relearn. Thus the claimed stability-plasticity resolution is only partially evaluated.

The real-language results are weak evidence for improved memory capacity. The evaluated commonsense tasks generally use short prompts and do not isolate long-context retrieval. The paper offers no long-context language-modeling, needle/retrieval, length-extrapolation, or controlled interference evaluation. Attributing the LAMBADA gains to superior memory retention is therefore speculative.

The language-modeling improvements are small and lack uncertainty estimates or repeated runs. At 760M, fine-tuning improves average commonsense accuracy over the corresponding non-metaplastic variants by only about 0.45–0.63 points. No confidence intervals or significance analysis are provided, so these differences may reflect run variance.

The results do not support an unqualified claim of consistent improvement. At 170M, fully trained Palimpsa-D scores 43.45 on average versus 43.91 without metaplasticity and 43.80 for Transformer++; fully trained Palimpsa-M also trails Transformer++. Even the best 170M fine-tuned result improves over its non-metaplastic counterpart by only 0.05 points.

The theoretical framing sometimes overstates what is obtained. The exact Gaussian posterior has key-induced off-diagonal precision terms; Palimpsa discards these terms in both precision and mean updates. The recurrence is consequently an architectural approximation, not exact Bayesian inference. The Mamba2 limiting argument additionally keeps beta times the value finite while beta approaches zero, which is algebraically possible but weakens the probabilistic interpretation and deserves more careful qualification.

The comparisons do not cleanly separate metaplasticity from other architectural choices. Palimpsa-D differs from Gated DeltaNet by an additional beta projection and an intra-layer residual, while Palimpsa-M and Palimpsa-D use substantially different backbones and layer counts. Within-architecture ablations help, but no parameter/FLOP-matched ablation identifies the contribution of each change.

Significance is reduced by substantial computational cost. The paper reports approximately 1.5x to 3x slower training and about 4x slower isolated recurrent inference than Simple GLA. The claim that Palimpsa supports efficient edge deployment is not demonstrated with end-to-end latency, memory, or energy measurements.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript does not provide a Palimpsa code release, complete kernel implementation, tokenizer and data-processing specification, language-model context length and batch configuration, optimizer coefficients and weight decay, evaluation-harness details, or variance across large-model runs. The supplied recurrence and partial hyperparameter tables are helpful but insufficient to reproduce the 15B/30B-token results reliably.

Presentation has several precision issues: the limitations are scattered rather than systematically discussed; notation alternates between row- and column-oriented state updates; some MesaNet citations appear mismatched; and the appendix organization is inconsistent. More importantly, conclusions repeatedly use causal language such as “validating” superior long-range retention when the reported evaluations do not directly validate that mechanism.

Ethics concerns are limited for this architectural work, but the impact statement is one-sided. It asserts energy-efficient edge intelligence without supporting energy measurements and does not discuss the environmental cost of 30B-token training. These are disclosure weaknesses rather than severe ethical violations.

Overall, the idea is promising and the synthetic evidence is encouraging, but unsupported central claims, non-diagnostic language evaluations, absent statistical evidence at scale, incomplete reproducibility, and a large efficiency penalty currently outweigh the contribution. Major experimental and claims-level revisions are needed before others can reliably build on it.

strengths: Soundness: Palimpsa is derived coherently from a discounted Bayesian linear-regression posterior, yielding interpretable mean and precision states. The paper clearly identifies the diagonal-precision approximation and provides detailed derivations and associative-scan equations.

Originality and significance: Applying Bayesian metaplasticity to fixed-state attention is a useful conceptual contribution. The unified view of Longhorn, DeltaNet, MesaNet, and Mamba2 is insightful, and converting a pretrained non-metaplastic model through short metaplastic fine-tuning is practically attractive.

Evaluation: The controlled MQAR experiments use eight seeds and show increasingly favorable metaplasticity effects as sequence length grows. At 760M parameters, both fine-tuned variants improve over their corresponding non-metaplastic versions under equal token budgets, with Palimpsa-D achieving the best reported average.

Presentation: The manuscript is well organized, motivates the stability-plasticity tradeoff clearly, and provides informative ablations, architectural details, hyperparameters, and an honest discussion of kernel bottlenecks.
Ethics: The work raises no evident material ethical concern, and its impact discussion appropriately emphasizes efficient fixed-memory inference.
weaknesses: The strongest empirical claims are not fully supported. Real-language gains are small—about 0.45 and 0.63 average accuracy points over the corresponding 760M ablations—and are reported without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. At 170M, fully trained metaplastic models are often no better and sometimes worse than their ablations.

The claimed expansion of long-context memory capacity is demonstrated mainly on curriculum-trained MQAR sequences up to length 1024. There are no capacity curves, length-extrapolation tests, or established long-context language benchmarks; the commonsense tasks do not directly isolate long-range memory, and LAMBADA perplexity alone is insufficient to establish superior retention.

Some theoretical language is too strong. The discounted posterior is a geometric-decay approximation rather than an actual sliding-window posterior, especially with input-dependent forgetting. Likewise, Mamba2 is recovered only in a limiting regime with nearly constant precision and a particular reparameterization, not as an unconditional exact special case. The claim that any non-metaplastic model can be transformed is broader than the demonstrated Mamba2/DeltaNet cases.

Efficiency is a substantial limitation: the appendix reports approximately 1.5–3× slower training and 4× slower isolated recurrent inference than Simple GLA. No end-to-end latency, peak-memory, or throughput comparison supports the abstract's claim of speed comparable to Mamba1.

Baseline coverage is incomplete. MesaNet is omitted because of implementation instability, and there is no matched comparison with several recent long-memory or test-time-learning approaches. Selecting the best MQAR learning rate using aggregate performance across seeds and sequence sizes also risks optimistic model-selection bias.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Many architectural and training settings are supplied, but the manuscript does not state that the custom Triton kernels and complete training code will be released, and it omits evaluation-harness versions, language-evaluation context settings, run-to-run variability, and several optimizer/fine-tuning details. These gaps matter because the reported language gains are small.

strengths: Originality: Recasting fixed-state in-context learning as a stability-plasticity problem and maintaining a second, per-state precision/importance variable is a creative synthesis of Bayesian continual learning and gated linear attention.

Significance: The proposed conversion of pretrained Mamba2 layers into metaplastic layers is practically interesting, especially because it avoids training the substantially slower Palimpsa architecture entirely from scratch.

Soundness: The weighted-posterior construction and full-covariance Gaussian derivation are developed clearly, and the manuscript explicitly identifies the diagonal-precision approximation used to obtain the implementable recurrence in Eq. 5.

Evaluation: The paper studies two architectural variants, includes direct metaplasticity ablations, evaluates models from 170M to 2.7B parameters, and uses eight seeds for MQAR. The improvement at long sequence lengths on MQAR and the 32k RULER variable-tracing result are promising evidence for improved retention.

Presentation: The paper is generally well organized, with readable equations, informative architectural diagrams, extensive hyperparameter tables, and a useful discussion of relationships to Longhorn, MesaNet, DeltaNet, and Mamba2.

Limitations and ethics: The authors honestly report unfavorable results, including degradation on several RULER tasks, the weakness of full-from-scratch training, register/HBM bottlenecks, and roughly 3-4x kernel slowdowns. The impact statement raises no material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: Palimpsa is not the exact variational solution claimed in parts of the presentation. The authors first solve the full-covariance posterior and then discard off-diagonal precision terms; this also changes the coupled mean solution. No approximation bound or comparison against the full solution is provided, so the Bayesian interpretation does not by itself establish that the implemented recurrence is well justified.

Soundness and specification: The Gaussian likelihood requires nonnegative beta values and the precision state must remain positive, yet the manuscript does not specify the activation or constraint used for beta in Palimpsa-D, nor clearly explain how positivity of all learned decay parameters is maintained. The assertion in Section 3.2 that I_min is always greater than I_prior therefore is not established from the stated architecture.

The claimed unification needs correction or clarification. Appendix Eq. 34 gives a previous-state correction term with coefficient beta, whereas Table 1's Gated DeltaNet rule gives coefficient alpha times beta. The unspecified 'right reparameterization' does not obviously reconcile both the correction and additive terms. Likewise, Mamba2 is only an asymptotic case when the learned precision remains near its prior, rather than an unconditional exact special case.

The language-model evidence is not statistically convincing relative to the small gains. Improvements in average commonsense accuracy are about 0.6-0.8 points, but no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. At 170M, fully trained metaplastic models frequently underperform their non-metaplastic counterparts. The fine-tuning comparisons also need a control that restarts the same checkpoint and learning-rate schedule while keeping metaplasticity disabled.

The long-context conclusions overstate mixed results. Full RULER results show that Palimpsa is substantially worse on variable tracing at 4k-16k, generally worse on single-needle retrieval and aggregation, and clearly better at 32k mainly on variable tracing. Highlighting only variable tracing in Table 3 does not establish broadly superior long-context memory. LongBench gains are modest, lack uncertainty, and the 'medium (32k-128k)' interpretation is insufficiently explained given training only up to 32k.

Efficiency weakens the practical contribution: Appendix A.12 reports approximately 3x training overhead at 760M and Appendix A.13 reports approximately 4x attention-kernel inference slowdown. This conflicts with the abstract's suggestion of speeds comparable to Mamba1, for which no direct benchmark is shown.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate. The Code Availability section ends after 'Our code is available at' with no link. The custom Triton kernels are consequently unavailable, and important details are missing for beta/decay parameterization, language-model random seeds, evaluation harness settings, long-data mixture proportions, instruction-tuning hyperparameters, and selection of the b_scale initialization.

Presentation and limitations: The writing is polished but repeatedly uses stronger causal language such as 'confirms' and 'directly validates' than the evidence supports. Limitations are scattered rather than synthesized, and the impact discussion omits the substantial training cost and energy implications of the reported slowdowns. Overall, the idea is promising, but these theoretical inconsistencies, mixed evidence, and reproducibility gaps require substantial revision before others can reliably build on it.

strengths: Originality/significance: Casting fixed-state in-context learning as Bayesian continual learning and introducing a per-state precision variable is an interesting synthesis of metaplasticity, online regression, and gated linear attention. The resulting dual-state recurrence could be useful beyond the particular architectures studied.

Evaluation: The paper spans synthetic recall, 170M/760M language models, and a 2.7B model-surgery experiment. The metaplastic versus non-metaplastic ablations are relevant, and MQAR reports eight seeds.

Presentation: The paper is generally readable and visually polished. It honestly reports some unfavorable findings, including weaker fully trained variants, short-context RULER regressions, and substantial implementation overhead.
weaknesses: Soundness: The evidence does not support the paper's broad claims of consistently or significantly expanding memory capacity. MQAR improvements are modest with visibly overlapping variation; at 170M, the best average score improves only from 43.91 to 43.96 within the Palimpsa-D pair, while fully trained metaplastic variants often regress. No significance tests or uncertainty are supplied for the language-model results.

The long-context evidence is distinctly mixed. The 2.7B model improves LongBench overall only from 19.3 to 20.4 and loses on the short category. In full RULER results it loses many single-needle, variable-tracing, and aggregation comparisons; the headline conclusion relies heavily on one 32k variable-tracing result, 24.4 versus 14.9, despite severe regressions at 4k and 8k.

Experimental selection and variance are insufficiently controlled. MQAR chooses the best learning rate 'across seeds and sequence sizes' without a clearly separated validation protocol. Language-model experiments provide no training seeds, confidence intervals, or evidence that sub-point average-accuracy gains exceed run-to-run variation.

Efficiency comparisons weaken the practical significance. Palimpsa doubles the recurrent state with an importance matrix, is reported as 1.5–3 times slower than Simple GLA in training and about 4 times slower at attention-only inference, yet the abstract says speeds are comparable to Mamba1 without presenting that benchmark. Token-matched comparisons are not compute-matched, and memory consumption and end-to-end latency are not reported.

The theoretical framing is overclaimed. Mamba2 is only recovered as an approximate limiting parameterization in which importance remains near its prior and low importance is offset by rescaled values; this does not establish that Mamba2 generally performs Bayesian inference. Likewise, experiments cover Mamba2- and DeltaNet-derived designs, not the claimed transformation of 'any non-metaplastic model.' The diagonal approximation also discards correlations central to the exact Bayesian solution, but its approximation error is never analyzed.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the claims. The Code Availability field contains no URL. Important details are missing, including dataset-mixture weights, much of the 2.7B optimization and instruction-tuning setup, evaluation prompts/settings, checkpoint access, language-model seeds, and sufficient kernel information to reproduce the efficiency results.

Limitations and ethics: The paper acknowledges systems overhead and some negative results, but does not adequately discuss statistical uncertainty, compute-normalized comparisons, the limited support for the claimed mechanism, or the doubled recurrent-state cost. The impact statement is mostly promotional. No major research-ethics concern is apparent, but the evidential and reproducibility gaps are substantial enough to prevent acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The proposed dual-state update has a coherent Bayesian motivation, and the manuscript provides substantial derivations connecting its mean and precision recurrences to gated linear-attention mechanisms. The MQAR ablations directly compare metaplastic and non-metaplastic variants across eight seeds and show that the advantage generally grows with sequence length.

Originality: Applying Bayesian metaplasticity to fixed-size in-context memory is a novel and insightful synthesis of continual learning and efficient sequence modeling. The interpretation of several existing recurrent attention models through a shared stability-plasticity framework is valuable even beyond the specific architecture.

Significance: Converting pretrained Mamba2 models through limited metaplastic fine-tuning is practically appealing. Results span synthetic recall, 170M/760M language models, and a surgically modified 2.7B model, suggesting that the idea is not confined to a toy setting.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear and well organized. Its diagrams, update-rule comparison, architectural appendix, and explanation of learning dynamics make a technically dense contribution accessible.

The authors discuss important unfavorable results rather than hiding them, including slower training and inference, the underperformance of fully trained variants, and degradation on several RULER tasks. The impact statement raises no material ethical concern for this work.
weaknesses: Soundness: Several headline claims are stronger than the evidence. The claimed approximately 5x memory expansion is inferred from where per-position WikiText NLL crosses a Transformer baseline, without uncertainty estimates or a direct capacity measurement. The 2.7B RULER evidence is mixed: Palimpsa improves Variable Tracing at 32k but is substantially worse at 4k–16k and loses on many single-needle and aggregation evaluations.

The language-model improvements are modest—roughly 0.6–0.8 average accuracy points—and no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. Consequently, it is difficult to separate consistent architectural gains from training variance at these scales.

The assertion that Mamba2 is a special case of Palimpsa is only an asymptotic correspondence under nearly constant importance, together with a reparameterization that keeps beta small while compensating through the value. This is informative but should be stated more narrowly than an exact architectural special-case result.

Comparisons equalize parameters and token counts but not computation. The appendix reports approximately 1.5x–3x training overhead and about 4x isolated recurrent-kernel inference slowdown, so the small downstream gains are not demonstrated to be compute-efficient. Stronger comparisons under matched FLOPs or wall-clock budgets are needed.

The empirical baseline set is limited: MesaNet is omitted, and there are no comparisons with other recent long-context or test-time-memory approaches. For the 2.7B experiment, only eight hand-selected layers are replaced, leaving unclear how sensitive gains are to layer choice, replacement count, or added state capacity.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted artifact. Although many architectural details are supplied, the code-availability entry contains no accessible link, and important large-scale details such as data-mixture proportions, optimization settings, hardware/compute, evaluation implementation, and variation across runs are missing. The custom Triton kernel is also essential to reproducing the reported system behavior.
